content: The quality of the randomized controlled trial (RCT) literature was deemed very low due to significant imprecision caused by the small number of events and indirectness. This indirectness arose from comparing patients initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) at CD4 counts below 350 cells/µL to those starting therapy at counts above 500 cells/µL. Similarly, the quality of observational studies was also very low, primarily due to the lack of adjustment for confounding factors and the small number of events. A subanalysis was conducted on patients who initiated ART at CD4 counts below 500 cells/µL (from both study arms) and those in the intervention arm who started ART between 500 and 550 cells/µL. Investigators found no significant differences between treatment arms for any of the reported critical outcomes. For most outcomes, except for grade 3/4 laboratory abnormalities, the quality of the RCT literature was low due to the small number of events and imprecise estimates. However, the quality of evidence for grade 3/4 laboratory abnormalities was moderate, though downgraded due to the relatively small number of events. The observational studies reviewed also had low-quality evidence, with no major study limitations other than their observational design. However, no additional factors improved the overall quality of the evidence. The studies included populations such as injection drug users, commercial sex workers, transgender individuals, and men who have sex with men. All three RCTs adequately described the randomization process and ensured allocation concealment. Follow-up was sufficient in all studies, and no reporting bias due to selective outcome reporting was identified. Observational studies did not suffer from obvious selection bias, and their populations were generally representative of average HIV-infected individuals, with participants drawn from the same community. Treatment data were obtained from healthcare records, and outcomes of interest were not present at baseline. The comparability between intervention and control arms was weak, as many studies did not adjust for confounding factors such as age or sex. Outcomes were assessed appropriately in all studies, either through independent blinded assessment or record linkage. Moderate-quality evidence was found supporting early ART initiation in asymptomatic HIV-infected patients with baseline CD4 counts of ≥500 cells/µL, which was associated with a lower risk of death, severe HIV infection, or malignancy. Observational studies also suggested that early ART initiation reduced the risk of HIV disease progression, though this evidence was of very low quality. Additionally, an RCT indicated that early ART initiation reduced the risk of HIV transmission, but this evidence was also of very low quality. Current WHO ART guidelines rate the quality of evidence for this outcome as high, but these recommendations were based on studies of serodiscordant couples where the infected partner had CD4 counts ≥350 cells/µL. The evidence is less robust for infected partners with CD4 counts ≥500 cells/µL, although efficacy estimates are similar. Moderate-quality evidence from an RCT showed that early ART initiation was not associated with an increased risk of grade 3/4 adverse events. However, low-quality evidence from an observational study suggested an increased risk of liver-related adverse events, though the clinical significance of this finding remains unclear, especially given conflicting RCT results. This review has several limitations. As with all systematic reviews, the findings are only as reliable as the identified literature. To minimize the risk of missing key studies, four targeted scientific databases were searched, and bibliographies of included studies and recent conference abstracts were reviewed. However, most of the identified literature originated from Europe, North America, and Australia, with limited data from Africa and Asia, reducing the generalizability of the findings to regions with the greatest need. The identified RCTs used data from the same study population (TEMPRANO), and the incidence of major clinical outcomes was particularly low, leading to imprecise mortality estimates. Consequently, the overall quality of RCT evidence for mortality was downgraded. Due to the lack of RCT data, cohort studies were also examined. According to GRADE criteria, cohort studies generally provide lower-quality evidence due to residual confounding. Additionally, the overall effectiveness estimates may have been biased due to a lack of independence between study populations. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to minimize this issue by removing studies with overlapping populations. For example, mortality was examined using three studies with minimal overlap: one from Italy, one large cohort from North America, and another large cohort primarily from Europe. The lack of independence between study populations did not significantly affect point estimates, but variability decreased with larger sample sizes. A more robust approach to synthesizing these data would involve conducting individual patient data meta-analyses for each outcome variable. Cohort studies are also prone to biases, including confounding and lead-time bias. Despite these limitations, the findings provide evidence supporting the benefits of initiating ART at CD4 counts of 500 cells/µL and above compared to later initiation when CD4 counts fall below 500 cells/µL. This effect was demonstrated for the combined risk of death, severe HIV disease, or incident malignancy, as well as for the risks of HIV disease progression and HIV transmission to an uninfected partner. The evidence regarding severe adverse events was mixed. An RCT found no differences in grade 3/4 laboratory abnormalities, while an observational study reported an increased risk of severe laboratory adverse events, particularly hepatic events, in the early treatment group. Ongoing RCTs, such as the Strategic Timing of Antiretroviral Treatment (START), ANRS 12249, PopART, SEARCH, and additional analyses from TEMPRANO, are expected to provide further evidence to definitively address the question of when to start ART, both at the individual and population levels.
